label: Confined spaces: pits, tanks, wells, silos
summary: Septic tanks, manholes, sewage lift stations, wells and well pits, cisterns, manure pits, silos, tanks and drink-CO2 cellars can hold air with too little oxygen, or with hydrogen sulphide, carbon dioxide or methane. You often can't see or smell it, and high levels kill in seconds. More than 60% of the people who die in confined spaces are would-be rescuers.
signs: Any pit, tank, vault, well, bin, silo or manhole that isn't built for people to stay in and has a tight way in or out. It needn't be small. For silos and grain bins, see Grain bins, hoppers and silos
Septic tanks: the gases inside can kill, and the methane can explode. Take great care even looking in
Sewage lift stations (below-ground chambers where drains collect and get pumped up), sumps and manholes: wastewater can leave them short of oxygen and full of toxic gas
Manure pits, tanks and tankers, and the barn room over an under-floor pit. Hydrogen sulphide sits just above the manure and reaches deadly levels within seconds of stirring or pumping

Wells in pits, pump houses and basements: on low-pressure days a well can breathe out air with very little oxygen. Rusting metal in a long-shut pit, and an empty cistern or tank, can use up the oxygen too
Basements and other low rooms where bars and restaurants keep CO2 for drinks. CO2 is 1.5 times heavier than air, pools at floor level and can kill even when oxygen is normal (see Compressed gas)
'Danger, Deadly Gases' or confined-space signs, and a rotten-egg smell. No smell proves nothing: CO2 and methane have none, and strong hydrogen sulphide numbs your nose
do: Work from outside wherever you can: pump, rake or fish things out through the opening rather than climbing in

Test the air from outside before anyone goes in, top to bottom, and keep testing: oxygen at least 19.5%, CO2 under 5,000 ppm (0.5%), and no alarm for hydrogen sulphide, carbon monoxide or flammable gas

Blow fresh air to the bottom with a fan or blower before entry and keep it running while anyone is inside; for a silo, at least 30 minutes first, longer for one wider than 7.2 m (24 ft). Never blow in bottled oxygen: it feeds fire
Anyone going in wears a full-body harness on a line to the outside, with a partner at the opening who watches the whole time and can haul them out without going in
Air out drink-CO2 cellars and coolers from the bottom: draw air out low and let fresh air in high
Get out at once if you start breathing fast or feel clumsy, tired, dizzy or headachy inside
dont: Don't go in after someone who has collapsed, not even for a moment: more than 60% of confined-space deaths are would-be rescuers, and farm pits and silos have killed several people at once this way
Don't assume an empty tank, pit or tanker is safe: gas stays behind, and hydrogen sulphide sits at the bottom even with the top hatch open
Don't stir, pump or agitate manure or sludge while anyone is in, over or beside the space
Don't clear a CO2 room with an oxygen reading alone: CO2 can be dangerous while oxygen still reads normal
Don't run a petrol pump, generator or heater in the space or at its opening without fresh air blowing through: its carbon monoxide builds up there (see Carbon monoxide)
Don't smoke or bring flames, sparks, work lights or power tools near a septic tank or manure storage: the methane can explode
ppe: Dust masks, filter masks and cartridge respirators don't add oxygen and are no use here. Only air-supplied breathing apparatus (SCBA or an air line) works in oxygen-poor air, and SCBA needs real training
A full-body harness and lifeline, so the person outside can pull you out

A gas meter for oxygen, hydrogen sulphide and flammable gas, with a hose and pump to sample from outside. Bump-test it before each day's use; that checks the alarms, not accuracy, and some meters stop working once calibration expires
firstAid: Rescue from outside only: haul them out on their lifeline, or blow fresh air in hard and wait. Fresh air helps them as well as you
Once they're out in fresh air, check breathing and start CPR if they aren't breathing normally
After hydrogen sulphide, silo gas or ammonia, a cough, breathlessness or chest pain can get worse over the following hours: keep them resting and watched; they need medical care
